claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy has greater atomic-scale chemical disorder than its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets.
Greater chemical disorder in the quinary alloy produces larger local lattice distortions than in the quaternary and ternary subsets.
Enhanced local lattice distortions lower the local stacking-fault energy.
Enhanced local lattice distortions modify dislocation mobility.
Enhanced local lattice distortions increase dislocation pinning.
Lower stacking-fault energy alters the balance between dislocation glide and deformation twinning.
The quinary alloy has increased twinning or secondary-slip activity relative to the quaternary and ternary subsets.
Enhanced lattice distortions reorder or otherwise change the active slip systems.
Changes in pinning, slip, and twinning increase the work-hardening rate of the quinary alloy.
The quinary alloy will exhibit a later onset of localized necking than the quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary alloy will exhibit greater overall ductility than the quaternary and ternary subsets.
Identical thermomechanical processing can produce single-phase FCC microstructures in the quinary alloy and the selected quaternary and ternary subsets.
The proposed mechanism applies at room temperature and moderate strain rate when all compared alloys remain single-phase FCC.
Processing defects, alternative phases, or substantial temperature or strain-rate changes may invalidate the proposed relationship.
Prior studies in complex alloys support a qualitative effect of lattice distortion on stacking-fault energy and dislocation behavior.
The alloys should be compared using identical processing histories and room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests, with microscopy and atom-scale characterization.

Absence of statistically higher strain hardening, delayed necking, altered dislocation or twinning behavior, or a correlation between lattice distortion and stacking-fault energy would falsify the proposed primary mechanism.
